evals.name: diagnose-stuck-at-the-chasm
evals.prompt: I'm the CEO of a Series A vertical AI startup. ~30 people, $3M ARR, growing but plateauing. Over the last 18 months we've won 8 great customers — Chief Innovation Officers at big-name firms who love us and give us keynote slots. But our pipeline is stalling — new prospects (usually the actual line-of-business owners, not innovation offices) take 6+ months to evaluate and mostly end in 'let's revisit next year'. Our sales cycles are getting *longer*, not shorter. Help me think about what's going on using Geoffrey Moore.
evals.expected_output: Output should: (a) diagnose this as classic chasm symptoms — visionary early customers (Chief Innovation Officer = classic visionary buyer), pragmatists (line-of-business owners) refusing to buy on visionary references, sales cycles lengthening instead of shortening; (b) name that they're at the chasm, not still in Early Market; (c) explain WHY pragmatists won't take visionary references (specific mechanism, not generic); (d) walk through the D-Day discipline required to cross — pick a beachhead segment, ship whole product for that segment, don't chase more visionary logos; (e) probably name Documentum as the archetype; (f) ask what evidence they have about what specific broken process is currently costing pragmatist buyers real money; (g) cite Moore (3rd ed 2014 book, or Lenny Podcast Jan 2024) at least once; (h) NOT confuse with Christensen's disruption theory.
assertions: Output diagnoses the situation as being at the chasm (not still in Early Market, not in Bowling Alley)
Output identifies Chief Innovation Officers as visionary buyers and line-of-business owners as pragmatist buyers, or equivalent psychographic labeling
Output explains that pragmatists will not accept visionary references — the specific mechanism, not generic advice
Output introduces D-Day / beachhead discipline as the corrective playbook
Output pushes back on continuing to chase visionary logos
Output names a compelling-reason-to-buy inquiry — asks what quantified broken-process pain the pragmatist buyer currently suffers
Output cites Geoffrey Moore, Crossing the Chasm (with edition, ideally 3rd ed 2014), or a specific source (podcast/blog/essay) at least once
Output does NOT confuse this with Christensen's Innovator's Dilemma or disruption theory
Output does NOT recommend a broad-front invasion (multiple verticals) as the fix
Output ends with a question that forces the user to name what stage they're actually in, what evidence tells them that, or what the compelling reason to buy is

evals.name: critique-mixing-playbooks-during-tornado
evals.prompt:
Here's our GTM plan for FY 2027. We're a SaaS platform in a category that's growing 60% year-over-year and every enterprise seems to be evaluating one of us or our top 3 competitors. Please critique this against Moore's framework.

---
FY2027 GTM PLAN

1. Deepen customer success — invest in high-touch onboarding, dedicated CSMs, quarterly business reviews
2. Verticalize into 3 new industries: healthcare, financial services, manufacturing — each with dedicated sales pods and industry-specific solution architects
3. Introduce customized deployment options and industry-specific SKUs
4. Improve NPS from 42 to 60
5. Focus on retention and net revenue retention (target NRR: 130%)
6. Add solution consultants to help enterprises tailor the product to their workflows
7. Deepen partnerships with regional systems integrators
---
evals.expected_output: Output should identify this as a Bowling Alley / Main Street playbook being run during what sounds like a Tornado (60% category growth, top-of-mind evaluation across all enterprises). Specifically it should: (a) name that if the category is in a Tornado, this plan is playing the WRONG stage — the Tornado playbook reverses Bowling Alley discipline (standardize, ship product not solutions, grab share above margin, kill customization); (b) name the specific plays that are stage-wrong (verticalization with customization, customer intimacy focus, NRR optimization); (c) warn about the consequence — ceding horizontal share to a rival that standardized faster (Chimp trajectory instead of Gorilla); (d) probably reference Inside the Tornado's stage-reversal doctrine; (e) also acknowledge — if they're NOT actually in a Tornado, this plan may be right, but then challenge whether the evidence supports Tornado; (f) offer the diagnostic questions to test tornado readiness.
assertions: Output diagnoses that this plan is running Bowling Alley / Main Street plays, potentially in a Tornado
Output identifies the specific plays that reverse under Tornado discipline — customization, verticalization, customer intimacy, NRR focus
Output introduces the stage-reversal doctrine from Inside the Tornado ('the winning strategy actually reverses the prior strategy')
Output names the risk — ceding horizontal share, Chimp vs. Gorilla outcome, or equivalent share-loss framing
Output challenges whether they are actually in a Tornado, or asks for the evidence (competitors in every deal, horizontal deals closing on features/price, standardization pressure from buyers)
Output cites Moore — Inside the Tornado (1995), Crossing the Chasm, or a specific source
Output does NOT accept the plan uncritically and just optimize the mechanics
Output does NOT recommend adding OKRs, more marketing, or more customer success as the fix

evals.name: ai-adoption-nuanced-use-case-diagnosis
evals.prompt: I'm a founder pitching investors on our agentic AI product for enterprise customer service call centers. Investors keep pushing back saying 'agentic AI has already crossed the chasm — you're too late'. How would Geoffrey Moore think about this?
evals.expected_output: Output should: (a) name that Moore, as of Feb 2026 Diginomica piece, has EXPLICITLY said agentic AI has NOT yet crossed the chasm — customer service call centers is one of the beachheads he named as moving toward crossing but not yet across; (b) apply Moore's use-case-by-use-case distinction — category chasm ≠ use-case chasm; AI-as-a-category has crossed for narrow use cases (HFT, digital ad placement, financial regulatory compliance per Forbes Jul 2024) but that does NOT mean agentic AI as a whole has crossed; (c) name the specific diagnostic Moore uses — trapped value large enough to force complete function re-engineering ('when one function completely re-engineers itself'); (d) push back on the investor framing as based on a category-level narrative that Moore's own framework rejects; (e) give the founder specific evidence to counter — the Feb 2026 Diginomica interview and the trapped-value discriminator; (f) probably cite Forbes/Randy Bean Jul 2024 and Diginomica Feb 2026 by name.
assertions: Output names that Moore has explicitly stated agentic AI has NOT crossed the chasm as of Feb 2026
Output applies the use-case-by-use-case distinction — some AI use cases have crossed, not the whole category
Output introduces 'trapped value' as Moore's discriminator variable
Output cites Moore's Feb 2026 Diginomica piece or Forbes/Randy Bean Jul 2024 interview specifically
Output pushes back on the investor's broad 'agentic AI has crossed' framing
Output distinguishes between use-case-level chasm crossings and category-level chasm crossings
Output does NOT parrot the 'AI is table stakes / too late' narrative

Output gives the founder actionable framing — either 'you're not too late because the specific use case hasn't crossed' or 'here's the evidence that would let you diagnose whether YOUR specific use case has crossed'
Output offers or references Moore's own 2024–2026 essays as counter-evidence to the investor's framing
